meta.titre: Latitude and Longitude: parallels, meridians, great circles and angular distance
meta.sous_theme: Parallels, meridians, great circles, giving positions and distances along a meridian

sections.contenu_markdown: A ship's captain in the Gulf of Guinea reports its position to the port with just two numbers: how far it is north of the equator and how far it is east of the Prime Meridian. Those two numbers are enough to fix any place on the Earth. Paper 1 tests the lines of the globe with short questions: which line is at a given value, which lines are great circles and why great circles matter. If you know the few rules of the grid, these questions become quick marks.

items: A full circle measures 360 degrees and a half circle 180 degrees.
The Earth is a sphere that turns around an axis joining the North Pole and the South Pole.
The equator is the imaginary circle around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the poles.

sections.titre: The grid of the globe and great circles
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Latitude and parallels
**Latitude** is the angle north or south of the equator, from $0^\circ$ at the equator to $90^\circ$ at each pole. Lines of latitude are **parallels**. They run east to west, never meet, and get shorter towards the poles.

| Parallel | Value |
|---|---|
| Equator | $0^\circ$ |
| Tropic of Cancer | $23\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ N |
| Tropic of Capricorn | $23\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ S |
| Arctic Circle | $66\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ N |
| Antarctic Circle | $66\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ S |

### Longitude and meridians
**Longitude** is the angle east or west of the **Prime Meridian**, $0^\circ$, which passes through Greenwich in London. Lines of longitude are **meridians**. They run from pole to pole, are all the same length, and come together at the poles. Longitude goes from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ east and west. The $180^\circ$ meridian lies on the opposite side of the Earth.

### Great circles
A **great circle** is a circle on the surface of the Earth whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth, so it divides the globe into two equal halves.
- The **equator** is the only parallel that is a great circle. Every other parallel is a small circle.
- Two meridians that are opposite each other form a great circle. A longitude of $x^\circ$ E pairs with $(180 - x)^\circ$ W, and the reverse.

**Importance:** a great circle gives the shortest route between two places, so aircraft and ships use it; it divides the Earth into hemispheres; and it is used in navigation and for measuring distances.

### Giving positions
Always give **latitude first**, then longitude, each with N, S, E or W. The whole of Cameroon lies north of the equator and east of the Prime Meridian.

variantes.nom: Finding the longitude that makes a great circle
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives one meridian and asks for its partner
variantes.contenu_markdown: Subtract the longitude from $180^\circ$ and change the side (east becomes west, west becomes east). For $15^\circ$ E the pair is $(180 - 15)^\circ = 165^\circ$ W. The Prime Meridian pairs with $180^\circ$, and $90^\circ$ E pairs with $90^\circ$ W.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When two places lie on the same meridian or the same parallel
variantes.contenu_markdown: If two places are on the same side of the equator, **subtract** their latitudes; if they are on opposite sides, **add** them. Along a meridian, $1^\circ$ of latitude is about 111 km, so distance = number of degrees $\times$ 111 km. The same rule works for longitudes on the same side of the Prime Meridian (subtract) or on opposite sides (add), but distances between meridians shrink towards the poles.

variantes.nom: Why a parallel is not a shortest route
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for the best route between two places on the same parallel
variantes.contenu_markdown: On a globe, the shortest route between two places on the same parallel other than the equator is not along that parallel. It is along a great circle, which curves towards the nearer pole. This is why long flights seem to curve on a flat map.

sections.enonce_markdown:
(a) Find the longitude that forms a great circle with $38^\circ$ E.
(b) Town A is at $12^\circ$ N and town B is at $7^\circ$ S on the same meridian. Calculate the distance between them, taking $1^\circ$ of latitude as 111 km.
(c) Is the parallel $12^\circ$ N a great circle? Give a reason.

etapes.justification: A great circle is made of two opposite meridians whose values add up to $180^\circ$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $180 - 38 = 142$, and the side changes from east to west.

etapes.action: Find the angle between the towns for part (b).
etapes.justification: One town is north and the other south of the equator, so the angles are added.
Each degree of latitude along a meridian is about 111 km.
Only the equator among the parallels has its plane through the centre of the Earth.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) $38^\circ$ E forms a great circle with **$142^\circ$ W**. (b) The towns are **2,109 km** apart. (c) **No.** The $12^\circ$ N parallel is a small circle because it does not divide the Earth into two equal halves; only the equator among the parallels is a great circle.

items.erreur_markdown: "$20^\circ$ E and $20^\circ$ W form a great circle."
items.pourquoi_faux: These two meridians are only $40^\circ$ apart. A great circle needs meridians on opposite sides of the Earth, with values adding to $180^\circ$.

items.erreur_markdown: "Every parallel of latitude is a great circle."
items.pourquoi_faux: A great circle must divide the Earth into two equal halves. Only the equator does so. Other parallels get smaller towards the poles.
items.correction_markdown: **Only the equator** is a parallel that is a great circle.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that lines of latitude meet at the poles.
items.pourquoi_faux: Parallels never meet. The lines that meet at the poles are the meridians, lines of longitude.
items.correction_markdown: **Meridians converge at the poles; parallels remain apart.**

items.erreur_markdown: Adding latitudes of two places on the same side of the equator, for example $9^\circ$ N and $4^\circ$ N giving $13^\circ$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The angle between places on the same side of the equator is the difference of their latitudes.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing a position as $9^\circ$ E, $4^\circ$ N or giving numbers without N, S, E or W.
items.pourquoi_faux: The usual order is latitude first, and the letters are needed to show the hemisphere.

items.enonce_markdown: State the value of (a) the Tropic of Capricorn, (b) the Arctic Circle, (c) the Prime Meridian. Which of these three is **not** a parallel?
items.solution_markdown: (a) **$23\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ S**. (b) **$66\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ$ N**. (c) **$0^\circ$** longitude. The Prime Meridian is the one that is not a parallel: it is a meridian, a line of longitude.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the longitude that forms a great circle with each of the following: (a) $75^\circ$ E, (b) $110^\circ$ W, (c) $0^\circ$, (d) $90^\circ$ E.

Town P is at $20^\circ$ N and town Q is at $65^\circ$ N on the same meridian. Town R is at $9^\circ$ N and town S at $5^\circ$ S on another meridian. Take $1^\circ$ of latitude as 111 km.
(a) Calculate the distance PQ and the distance RS.
(b) Explain why a flight between two places on the $50^\circ$ N parallel does not follow the parallel.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) PQ: both are north, so $65 - 20 = 45^\circ$ and $45 \times 111 = 4\,995$ km. RS: opposite sides of the equator, so $9 + 5 = 14^\circ$ and $14 \times 111 = 1\,554$ km. **PQ = 4,995 km; RS = 1,554 km.**
(b) The shortest route between two places is along a great circle. The $50^\circ$ N parallel is a small circle, so a flight along it would be longer. Aircraft follow a great circle that curves towards the pole.

items_markdown: Latitude is measured north and south of the equator (0 to 90 degrees); parallels run east to west and never meet.
Longitude is measured east and west of the Prime Meridian (0 to 180 degrees); meridians meet at the poles.
A great circle divides the Earth into two equal halves; the equator is the only parallel that is one.
Two meridians form a great circle when they are opposite: x degrees E pairs with (180 minus x) degrees W.
Great circles give the shortest route, divide the Earth into hemispheres and help in navigation.
Distance along a meridian = degrees of latitude difference (added across the equator) times 111 km.
